page_title: It's not what programming languages do, it's what they shepherd you to

sources.entry: It's not what programming languages do, it's what they shepherd you to

summary.title: It's not what programming languages do, it's what they shepherd you to
summary.one_liner: Programming languages and their ecosystems nudge developers toward whatever is easy in that language, even when a better-suited tool exists, and this "shepherding" explains why language debates go in circles.
keywords: blog post essay on programming languages
takeaways: Shepherding is an invisible property of a language and its ecosystem that steers people toward the approach that is easiest or most natural in that language.
The shepherded path may not be the best for maintainability, readability or performance, even when the language provides better tools.
Perl users often parse XML or HTML with regexes because text manipulation is easy in Perl while using an XML parser is not.
Debates like 'language X is bad' versus 'you can write good code in X' miss the point; the useful question is what the language pushes you toward.
Other examples cited include C pointer-based data handling, C++ header-only dependencies, Java's mandated classes, and Turing complete configuration languages.
summary.summary: The author opens with a common argument pattern about whether a programming language is bad, then proposes a name and definition for the underlying issue: "shepherding," the unconscious steering of developers toward solutions that are natural or easy in a given language. The post illustrates the idea with Perl users reaching for regexes on XML and HTML instead of available parsers, and Makefiles that embed shell pipelines. It then lists brief further examples involving C, C++, Java and configuration languages. The piece is a short conceptual essay with no code or tutorial steps.
